tasks.short: Interview a new patient and write the admission note.

steps.what: Read the admission card before this interview.
Interview new patients to assess their mental health status and to obtain their treatment history.
Complete admission forms from what the patient said.

tasks.design: A ward colleague writes a paper admission card with the patient name, the ward, and the form title. The technician reads it, interviews the patient, and writes the admission note by hand. The card does not hold the condition or the history.
tasks.previous_blocker: The ward list and the blank form sat in different places, so the search before the interview was slow.
tasks.enabler_now: A paper card names the row. The interview and the written note stay with the technician.
tasks.still_hard: What the patient means, and what belongs in the note, still depend on the person in the room.
tasks.human_edge: Only the technician can judge what the patient means and what to write down.
tasks.altitude: A card shortens finding the ward row. The technician still interviews the patient and writes the admission note.

reach.task: Interview a new patient and write the admission note
reach.learn: The card names the ward. The nurse still interviews and writes the note.

evidence.claim: A paper card with the patient name, the ward, and the form title shortens the search before the interview. The interview and the written note stay with the technician. Model knowledge of this design.

assumptions: The workplace is a mid-size European care ward.
A ward colleague writes the admission card before the interview.
Fields are the patient name, the ward, and the form title.
The admission card does not hold the patient's condition or treatment history.
The technician interviews the patient and writes the admission note at full time.
The written admission note is the technician's own writing for the care team. It is not posted anywhere else.
If the row is missing, the technician reads the paper ward list inside s1.
There is no native system to configure and no custom code.
Focal upkeep is zero because a ward colleague keeps the card, counted on the other line.
Staff consent for a monitoring or recording tool is out of scope because this design adds none.
unknowns: Whether this ward already keeps a one-line admission card for each new patient.
research_questions: How often a first interview has no row on the admission card.

incremental.description: No extra technician upkeep. A ward colleague keeps the admission card.
A ward colleague writes the admission card: patient name, ward, and form title.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The interview is the first one, so the admission card has no row and the technician reads the paper ward list. The search saving disappears.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Call a relative to arrange a family conference.

steps.what: Read the family card before this call.
Contact patients' relatives to arrange family conferences.
Write the agreed family conference time.

tasks.design: A ward colleague writes a paper family card with the patient name, the relative name, and the phone. The technician reads it, calls the relative, and writes the agreed time by hand. The card does not hold the patient's condition.
tasks.previous_blocker: The relative's phone sat apart from the ward list, so the search before the call was slow.
tasks.enabler_now: A paper card names the phone. The call and the written time stay with the technician.
tasks.still_hard: Whether the relative will agree a time still depends on the person on the phone.
tasks.human_edge: Only the technician can hear what the relative will agree and write that time.
tasks.altitude: A card shortens finding the phone. The technician still calls the relative and writes the agreed time.

reach.task: Arrange a time for a family conversation
reach.learn: The card names the phone. The representative still calls and writes the time.

evidence.claim: A paper card with the relative's name and phone shortens the search before the call. The call and the written time stay with the technician. Model knowledge of this design.

assumptions: The workplace is a mid-size European care ward.
A ward colleague writes the family card before the call.
Fields are the patient name, the relative name, and the phone.
The family card does not hold the patient's condition.
The technician calls the relative and writes the agreed time at full time.
The written conference time is the technician's own note. It is not posted anywhere else.
If the row is missing, the technician reads the paper ward list inside s1.
There is no native system to configure and no custom code.
Focal upkeep is zero because a ward colleague keeps the card, counted on the other line.
Staff consent for a monitoring or recording tool is out of scope because this design adds none.
unknowns: Whether this ward already keeps a one-line family card with a phone.
research_questions: How often a first call has no row on the family card.

incremental.description: No extra technician upkeep. A ward colleague keeps the family card.
A ward colleague writes the family card: patient name, relative name, and phone.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: The call is the first one, so the family card has no row and the technician reads the paper ward list. The search saving disappears.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The psychiatric technician still interviews new patients and writes the admission note, and still calls relatives and writes the agreed time. A card only shortens finding the ward row or the phone.
reach: Registered Nurses: interview one new patient after the card names the ward.
Patient Representatives: call one relative after the card names the phone.
skills_to_grow: Open the paper ward list when the card has no row.
Assess the patient from the interview, not from the card.
role.ambitious_version: Cards do not interview, assess, write the note, or call the relative. The psychiatric technician still does.
